To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the sensitivity of response ratios to reinforcement ratios increases with stimulus disparity, (2) sensitivity decreases systematically with successive time intervals since component alternation, and (3) sensitivity to stimulus disparity is greater in the first time interval than later time intervals.

the relative effectiveness of stimuli in controlling behavior is a joint function of the relative effectiveness of the reinforcers that maintain behavior in the presence of those stimuli and of the time since the stimuli were last presented together with different reinforcers.
sensitivity to reinforcement increases with increasing stimulus disparity and that this sensitivity increases with increasing time since the last component alternation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relative effects of stimulus and reinforcement on the sensitivity of behavior.
the relation between stimulus and reinforcer relavities in a multiple-schedule procedure.
the effects of the physical characteristics of stimuli on the relative effectiveness of stimuli as reinforcers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sensitivity to reinforcement is relative in both local and dimensional terms.
the sensitivity of response rates to reinforcer ratios is a function of the stimulus differences between the component stimuli.
sensitivity to reinforcement is a function of the time since reinforcement and of the extent to which reinforcement is associated with stimulus differences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of reinforcement on sensitivity to stimuli are relative to the stimuli themselves and to the history of reinforcement.

sensitivity to changes in reinforcement rate is a function of the extent to which reinforcement rate is related to the discriminative stimuli, the extent to which the stimuli differ from one another, and the time since the stimuli were last related to one another.
sensitivity to reinforcement is a product of the interaction between the relative reinforcement rates in the components and the relative discriminative stimuli in the components.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stimulus effects on behavior are not absolute and that they depend on the stimulus context in which they occur.
stimulus differences can affect sensitivity to reinforcement in multiple schedules in the same way that stimulus differences affect choice between concurrent schedules.

the relative effectiveness of a reinforcer depends not only on the amount of reinforcement it provides but also on the stimulus conditions under which it is delivered. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved).
